rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger's final declaration acquits him from the rejecters and signals that migration is approaching.
rows.anchor: Such a declaration is reported from every messenger in the final phase.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God the giver of death warns disbelievers that they will appear before Him for accountability.
rows.anchor: The words “the God Who gives you death” are meant to warn the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith means sincere devotion to the one God and abstention from every form of polytheism.
rows.anchor: The real feature of faith is sincere devotion to the one God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since only God can harm or benefit by His permission, invoking others is self-injustice and withholds God's greatest right.
rows.anchor: invoking others beside Him is an act of injustice on one’s own self

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse negates the grounds for idol worship and directs people to seek refuge in God, the sole forgiver and merciful one.
rows.anchor: people should seek refuge with God because it is He Who alone forgives and has mercy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though addressed to everyone, the final warning targets Quraysh; the Prophet must deliver truth, not force acceptance.
rows.anchor: The address here is general but it is directed at the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must follow revelation and persevere until God's judgment, which recalls the promised victory for messengers and believers in 10:103.
rows.anchor: This decree is referred to earlier in verse 103: ultimately, the Almighty grants victory to His messengers and believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd pairs with Yūnus: both share the Alif Lām Rā name and core theme, while differing in brevity, detail, and argument; Hūd expands the earlier concise accounts.
rows.anchor: this sūrah forms a pair with Sūrah Yūnus, there is no basic difference between the themes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening introduces revelation first in concise principles and later in detail, then calls people to worship God, repent, and heed the Prophet's warning and glad tidings.
rows.anchor: principles and basics were revealed at the beginning. They were presented with brevity and in concise form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecters act as if hiding from God, though He knows hidden and apparent things and every heart's secrets; He provides for all and records each creature's dwelling and burial place.
rows.anchor: He knows the hidden and the apparent and is also aware of the secrets of the hearts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The world is a test: respite emboldens wrongdoers to mock, while adversity makes people despair and blessings make them boast; the patient and grateful receive forgiveness and reward.
rows.anchor: God has created it to see how people behave

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When seized, people become dejected and hopeless; when spared, they boast, while few endure hardship patiently and receive the reward promised to the patient and grateful.
rows.anchor: When they are seized by God, they become dejected and lose hope; however, when they are given respite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not grieve over demands for miracles; the challenge to produce ten fabricated sūrahs exposes the Quraysh's inability and establishes the revelation's divine source and God's sole worship.
rows.anchor: ask them to bring ten such fabricated sūrahs and also ask for help from the associates

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who seek worldly pleasures receive their full due in this life, but have only Hell in the Hereafter and see their deeds annulled.
rows.anchor: those who desire the pleasures of this world are give everything in this wor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People whose nature remains sound recognize the Qur'an's call as their own and find support in Moses' Book; those spiritually blinded persist until they see Hell.
rows.anchor: Only they will accept faith who have protected their nature from perversion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unjust who invent lies about God and obstruct His path remain within His grasp and are given respite for full punishment in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: they are not beyond the grasp of God. However, God is giving them respite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only those who surrender to God, believe, and do good succeed; the parable of the blind and deaf versus those who see and hear shows the groups cannot be equal.
rows.anchor: The parable of both these groups is that of the blind and deaf and of those who have eyes and ears

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's story mirrors the Prophet's mission: his nation used Quraysh-like excuses and drowned; verse 49 assures the Prophet that steadfast believers will ultimately triumph.
rows.anchor: The warnings and glad tidings with which he came to his nation were precisely the same

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘Ād adopted toward Hūd the same attitude Noah's people and Quraysh showed their prophets, then met their fate while Hūd succeeded; the account warns Quraysh and reassures the Prophet.
rows.anchor: The anecdote of the nation of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accounts of Thamūd and Ṣāliḥ serve the same warning and reassurance purpose as the preceding prophetic histories.
rows.anchor: The anecdotes of the nations of Tham ūd and of Ṣāliḥ are narrated for precisely the same purpose

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot's story serves the same purpose; it also shows that Quraysh's demand for an angel is a call for doom, since angels arrive on major divine missions.
rows.anchor: the demand of the Quraysh to make an angel descend on them is actually a call for their doom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham was so apprehensive when the angels came that he remained uneasy until he learned their mission.
rows.anchor: He did not rest assured until he came to know the nature of their mission at hand

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage recounts the story of Shu‘ayb and the people of Madyan.
rows.anchor: The anecdote of Shu‘ayb (sws) and the people of Madyan is recounted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses and Pharaoh are mentioned briefly because the previous sūrah already related their story in detail.
rows.anchor: because it was related in detail in the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section states why the stories were told and guides the Prophet and companions; Quraysh must learn from local history or face the same consequences.
rows.anchor: The Quraysh are warned to learn a lesson from the history of their country

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah as a whole is a comprehensive sermon directed toward one prescribed purpose.
rows.anchor: the whole of it is a comprehensive sermon on a prescribed purpose

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘Ād matched the rebellious attitude of Noahs people and Quraysh, then met their fate while Hūd succeeded; this history warns Quraysh and reassures the Prophet.
rows.anchor: attitude with their prophet Hūd (sws) as the one adopted by the nation of Noah (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif Lām Rā is shared by Hūd and Yūnus, signaling similar subjects; Hūd elaborates matters treated concisely in its paired sūrah, especially prophetic stories, for teaching and instruction.
rows.anchor: The previous sūrah also has the same name. This signifies that the themes and subjects of both are similar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening word for the verses means making something tightly joined and strong; it describes the Qur'an's initially brief, comprehensive formulations, progressively explained into a full system of life.
rows.anchor: It is used for a cloth that is treated to make thick. The purpose of using this word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gradual Qur'anic elaboration serves instruction, unlike the Torah, most of which was revealed in one episode; God's wisdom condenses teaching and His knowledge unfolds its vast meanings.
rows.anchor: This way of gradual elaboration and elucidation was not adopted in the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The foundational message is worship of God alone; messengers bring mercy's glad tidings to those accepting it and warn the averse, and the Prophet's duty is to deliver both.
rows.anchor: The basic message of this Book is that people should not worship anyone except God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The glad tidings call people to seek their Lord's forgiveness and turn back to Him.
rows.anchor: people should seek forgiveness from their Lord and turn to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecters face the worldly calamity that destroys a people after a messenger fully conveys the truth, while believers receive respite and succeed; the passage also warns of punishment in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: totally wiped out by some horrible calamity once the truth is communicated to them in its ultimate form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance requires both asking forgiveness and promising to stop the sin, and turning to God by following His guidance; continued sin makes repeated repentance a joke.
rows.anchor: if a person does not desist from his sin and evade the right path, he may repent a hundred times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for turning chests means turning away and covering oneself, a posture of arrogance or hatred used to avoid listening.
rows.anchor: Another form of this is that a person covers himself with a piece of cloth and leaves that place

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A similar arrogant posture appears in the description in al-Ḥajj 22:9.
rows.anchor: Sūrah al-Ḥajj, this state of a person is described by the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's people similarly covered themselves with cloaks when called to repent, as described in 71:7.
rows.anchor: This is depicted in verse 7 of Sūrah Nūḥ thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant Quraysh turned away from the Prophet's warnings as if evasion could protect them; avoiding reality changes nothing, since God knows what is hidden and apparent, even beneath a covering.
rows.anchor: the arrogant Quraysh in response to the warnings of the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The terms for a creature's settled place and entrusted place mean its residence during life and its burial place; this elaborates God's knowledge and echoes 6:98.
rows.anchor: The former refers to the place where a person spends his life and the latter to his place of burial

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No creature can escape God, who knows where each creature lives and will be buried.
rows.anchor: This is actually a further explanation of the extent of God’s knowledge mentioned in the previous verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every creature receives its ordained provision wherever it lives, rebuking those who evade the words of the God whose provision sustains them.
rows.anchor: it is receiving its ordained sustenance from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the burial place an entrusted place subtly teaches that the dead are not obliterated: the earth holds them until it returns them to their Lord.
rows.anchor: no one should think that a person who has passed away has been obliterated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The open Book omits nothing and makes every item easy to find.
rows.anchor: nothing has been left out from the book and there will no botheration in finding anything from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse introduces the reward and punishment about which people were warned, but they mocked instead of preparing.
rows.anchor: instead of acknowledging it and preparing themselves for it, they made fun of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The six days are divine periods, each thousands of earthly days, and creation's gradual completion shows a planned, wise process rather than an accident.
rows.anchor: The six days referred to here are not six earth days; they are six days of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's throne signifies His rule: before land appeared, the earth was water under His governance; land and life then emerged, as Genesis also says, though its translators blurred the meaning.
rows.anchor: The word “throne” signifies the rule of God. Before land appeared on his earth, it was all water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ordered creation cannot be purposeless entertainment: human freedom and moral awareness show that life is a test, followed by accountability and judgment according to deeds.
rows.anchor: the freedom given to human beings in this world to exercise their will and their awareness of good and evil show that God is testing them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added phrase that creation tests who is best in deeds clarifies the purpose already mentioned in Yūnus.
rows.anchor: The universe being created in six days was also mentioned in Sūrah Yūnus earlier

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the Prophet explains resurrection for accountability, rejecters call it magic rather than recognizing its eloquence.
rows.anchor: they regard this statement to be magic instead of acknowledging it to be an epitome of eloquence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ummah here means a period, as it does in Yūsuf 12:45.
rows.anchor: A similar usage can be seen in verse 45 of Sūrah Yūsuf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After rejecters mock resurrection, they also mock the worldly punishment that follows rejecting a messenger, though it will engulf them and cannot be averted.
rows.anchor: This verse says that this attitude of mockery is also found in them regarding the torment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neither the rejecters nor their deities and intercessors can ward off the torment once it arrives.
rows.anchor: neither will they themselves be able to ward it off, nor will their deities and intercessors be able to do so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse says “a human being,” it means the people under discussion; a principle statement indirectly addresses a stubborn person more forcefully.
rows.anchor: Though a general word “human being” is used, it refers to the same people which are under discussion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People become ungrateful and despair when favor is withdrawn, then arrogant and boastful when it returns; they even demand promised punishment despite living on God's provisions.
rows.anchor: instead of being grateful at the provisions and sustenance God has provided them with, their conceit makes them make fun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers who do good are exceptions: hardship deepens their patience and hope in mercy, while favor makes them grateful and more righteous, earning forgiveness and reward.
rows.anchor: Hardships strengthen their patience and favours make them more righteous and grateful
